questions: Is /admin/auth/mfa/setup gated by anything beyond a bare valid access token (role check, MFA-satisfied check, password/current-code re-verification)?
Does AdminUser.stageMfaSecret() or confirmMfa() check whether MFA is already enabled before overwriting the secret / flipping the flag?
Is there any other layer (aspect, interceptor, DB constraint) that blocks re-enrollment of an already-MFA-enabled admin?
Is /admin/auth mounted at a path that AuthRateLimitFilter.bucketFor() actually matches (it only pattern-matches '/auth/...'), or does it fall through unthrottled?
Is there a compensating per-account lockout (independent of the IP filter) that already bounds password-guessing against a single admin identity?
Does that lockout also block spraying across many different admin accounts, or only repeated guesses against one account?
Is there an edge/proxy-level (Caddy/nginx) rate limit on /admin/auth/* that would compensate for the missing in-app bucket?
Does MeeraWorkspace.tsx's handlePay() ever receive a real campaign id, or is MEERA_DEMO_CAMPAIGN_ID truly hardcoded and unconditionally used?
Is MeeraWorkspace reachable in production without a mock/demo-mode gate (i.e., does /brand/meera route unconditionally render it)?
Does RequestPaymentExecutor's confirmActionUrl() point to a route that is actually registered in src/App.tsx, or does it 404 to the catch-all?
Is the request_payment Meera tool actually wired to a live, callable endpoint (not dead/unregistered code)?
Does ToolResultRenderer actually render confirmActionUrl as a clickable, same-origin link a real user would click?
Are there existing tests that already exercise any of these three paths, whose outcome would raise or lower confidence?

findings.title: Admin MFA secret can be overwritten while MFA is enabled (no current-code or password re-verification)
evidence: AdminAuthController.java:114-118 — POST /admin/auth/mfa/setup calls adminAuthService.setupMfa(principal) gated only by @AuthenticationPrincipal (any valid admin JWT), no role or MFA-satisfied check.

AdminAuthService.java:277-291 (setupMfa) — loads the admin, generates a brand-new TOTP secret, and calls admin.stageMfaSecret(...) unconditionally. No check of admin.isMfaEnabled() before overwriting, no requirement for the caller's current TOTP code or password.

AdminUser.java:242-245 (stageMfaSecret) — unconditionally overwrites encryptedMfaSecret and calls touch(); the entity itself enforces nothing about prior MFA state (by its own javadoc, 'the entity is a plain data holder').

AdminUser.java:247-251 (confirmMfa) — unconditionally sets mfaEnabled = true after any code check against the newly staged secret; no comparison against a previous secret or requirement of a currently-valid old code.

AdminContextService.java:82-108 — the only MFA gate that exists (requireMfaSatisfied) REJECTS calls when MFA is NOT YET enabled (403 MFA_SETUP_REQUIRED); it has no effect once MFA IS enabled, and setupMfa()/verifyMfa() do not call it at all — they call the bare requireAdminId().
No test file (grep of influora-api/src/test) exercises AdminAuthService#setupMfa at all, so this behavior is unverified even by the repo's own test suite.
findings.reasoning: The claim holds exactly as stated: an attacker holding any valid (even short-lived) admin access token can call POST /admin/auth/mfa/setup at any time — including on an account that already has MFA enabled — and it will silently overwrite the stored secret with a fresh one, then POST /admin/auth/mfa/verify with a code from the attacker's own authenticator to complete re-enrollment. No password re-entry, no current-TOTP challenge, no comparison against the old secret. This is a genuine persistence/account-takeover vector once an access token leaks (XSS, log leak, MITM, etc.). Not downgraded — I found no mitigating control anywhere in the call path.

findings.title: Admin login and refresh have no IP rate-limit bucket
evidence: AdminAuthController.java:56 — @RequestMapping("/admin/auth") — admin auth is mounted at /admin/auth, NOT /auth.

AuthRateLimitFilter.java:342-511 (bucketFor) — traced every branch for a POST to '/admin/auth/login' or '/admin/auth/refresh' (context-stripped path becomes '/admin/auth/login' etc.): none of the literal-path/prefix checks match ('/auth/refresh' equality fails, 'startsWith("/auth/")' fails because the path starts with '/admin/', not '/auth/'); execution falls through to 'return null' at line 511, meaning NO bucket is assigned and the filter lets the request through at doFilterInternal (lines 296-299) with zero rate limiting and no X-RateLimit-* headers at all.

grep of influora-api/src/test/security shows 12 AuthRateLimitFilter*BucketTest files covering every other bucket (tracking, meta-oauth, meera, client-errors, me-password, admin-coupon-issue, etc.) but NONE for /admin/auth/login or /admin/auth/refresh — this path was never even considered when the filter's extensive bucket list was built out, confirming it's a genuine gap, not an intentional exclusion.
deploy/hostinger/Caddyfile has no rate-limit directives at all (grep found only a comment about TLS cert issuance rate limits) — no edge/proxy-level compensating control.

REFUTING EVIDENCE (my own finding, not in the original claim): AdminSecurityProperties.java:38-39 (lockoutMaxAttempts=5, lockoutCooldownSeconds=900) + AdminUser.java:190-195 (recordFailedLogin) + AdminAuthService.java:118-131 (recordFailedAttemptAndThrow, invoked on every bad password) implement a PER-ACCOUNT lockout: after 5 failed password attempts against one admin email, that account locks for 15 minutes regardless of source IP. This is a real, already-shipped brute-force control on login that is completely independent of AuthRateLimitFilter.
findings.reasoning: The code-level fact is fully CONFIRMED: /admin/auth/login and /admin/auth/refresh really do fall through AuthRateLimitFilter unthrottled — this is not a misread of the claim. But the impact claim 'this allows unlimited password spraying' is overstated. Per-account lockout (5 attempts / 15 min, keyed by admin email, not IP) already bounds brute-forcing ANY SINGLE known admin account to ~20 guesses/hour regardless of how many IPs the attacker rotates through — that is not 'unlimited.' The 'deliberate lockout of admin accounts' consequence is also not really a product of the missing IP bucket: 5 failed attempts is already far below the 'sensitive' bucket's own default of 10/window, so even WITH IP throttling wired up, one wrong-password request per attempt from anywhere would still lock a known admin's account in 5 tries — that DoS property is inherent to the lockout design itself, not caused by this gap. What the missing bucket genuinely enables and the account-lockout does NOT cover: (a) unbounded ENUMERATION/spraying across many different admin email addresses (each gets its own 5-attempt budget, unbounded by IP), and (b) no volumetric/DoS throttle on /admin/auth/refresh, which has no analogous lockout and could be hit at high volume (though refresh tokens are high-entropy random values, so this is a resource-cost concern rather than a credential-guessing one). Net: real gap, worth fixing (defense-in-depth against multi-account spraying and refresh-endpoint volume), but not the P1 'unlimited password spraying' scenario as framed. Downgraded to P2.
findings.disagreement: The original claim's severity (P1) and its 'unlimited password spraying' framing are not supported once the existing per-account lockout (AdminSecurityProperties/AdminUser.recordFailedLogin) is accounted for. The underlying code gap (no bucket match) is accurately described and real.

findings.title: Meera brand funding flow has no working live path: demo campaign id plus link to a non-existent /brand/escrow route
evidence: MeeraWorkspace.tsx:21 — const MEERA_DEMO_CAMPAIGN_ID = 'meera_demo_campaign', with the file's own comment admitting: 'In live mode this must be the real campaign id threaded from the deal/collaboration context, not a constant.'

MeeraWorkspace.tsx:75-81 (handlePay) — const idempotencyKey = `${MEERA_DEMO_CAMPAIGN_ID}-${Date.now()}`; const res = await api.payments.fundEscrow(MEERA_DEMO_CAMPAIGN_ID, idempotencyKey) — unconditionally uses the hardcoded demo id, no prop/context threading a real campaign id anywhere in this component.

src/pages/brand-meera.tsx — BrandMeeraPage renders <MeeraWorkspace /> with no props and no mock/live gate; src/App.tsx:324-331 mounts this at /brand/meera unconditionally inside the normal authenticated brand route tree (BrandLayoutWrapper) — this is live, reachable production UI, not dead/demo-only code.
onPay={handlePay} is wired into <LivingCanvas> at both MeeraWorkspace.tsx:111 and :137 (desktop and mobile-sheet variants), i.e., a real Pay button in the funding stage invokes this handler.
RequestPaymentExecutor.java:181-183 (confirmActionUrl) — return "/brand/escrow/fund?campaignIntentId=" + campaignIntentId — verified this exact string is what's returned to the client.
ToolResultRenderer.tsx:283-292 — Confirm payment — the URL is rendered verbatim as a real, clickable same-origin link, not sanitized or resolved through any route table.

src/App.tsx — grepped every '/brand/...' <Route path=...> declaration (30+ routes enumerated): no '/brand/escrow' or '/brand/escrow/fund' route exists anywhere. The catch-all is <Route path="*" element={<NotFoundPage />} /> (App.tsx:883).

MeeraInternalController.java:245,257-258 confirms POST /request_payment is a live, tool-gated (requireTool) internal endpoint actually reachable by the production Meera agent pipeline — not unregistered/inert code.
findings.reasoning: Every element of this compound finding checks out independently against the exact cited lines, and I traced the consequences one step further than the original claim: (1) the Pay button in the live-mounted MeeraWorkspace always funds a fake campaign id regardless of which real deal/campaign the brand is in, and (2) the separate request_payment tool's 'Confirm payment' link — reachable via a live, tool-gated backend endpoint — points to a frontend path that was never registered in the router and definitively resolves to NotFoundPage. Both are real, reachable, committed defects that together mean there is no functioning way for a brand to complete an escrow funding action that originates from Meera. I did not find any compensating live-mode branch, feature flag, or alternate route that would make either path actually work in production.
